newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Buthelezi backs unity with Mandela's ANC.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Buthelezi backs unity with Mandela's ANC.

text.p: South Africa's top black opposition leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi on Sunday backed unity with the ruling African National Congress (ANC), long the arch foe of his Inkatha Freedom Party.
"I do not see why it should not happen," Buthelezi said in an interview with South Africa's Sunday Times newspaper, adding it would be "an ideal thing".

Buthelezi, an ANC member in the 1960s who broke with the movement in 1979 over its commitment at the time to armed struggle, said the ANC and his Inkatha Freedom Party had been driven apart by differences that were "not really necessary".
"There was a difference in strategy, not ideology," he said.
"I don't apologise for the fact that I come from the ANC stable."

ANC national chairman Jacob Zuma and his Inkatha counterpart Ben Ngubane are in the forefront of a peace initiative which has seen a significant thawing in relations between the parties over the past few months.

Buthelezi's support for the peace initiative is crucial but a political analyst based in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, Buthelezi's traditionalist Zulu powerbase, cautioned the comments could not be interpreted as a major step forward.

"Buthelezi's words, to me, are on the vague and lukewarm side. They don't represent a sharp change or a sign of progress," Alexander Johnston, politics professor at the University of Natal, told Reuters.

Johnston said Buthelezi could be seeking concession from the ANC on the role of traditional Zulu societies in rural areas, one of the key outstanding issues between the two parties which have been locked in a low-key civil war for over a decade.

"One of the critical issues between the two parties now that could stand in the way of a substantial and lasting peace...is whether to allow Inkatha the freedom from competition in rural areas," Johnston added.

Inkatha, which rules the KwaZulu-Natal government, draws its support from just over half of the province's nine million Zulus. It has repeatedly accused the central government of trying to undermine the long-term survival of traditional societies.
President Nelson Mandela has been actively courting support for his ANC in the region's rural areas in recent weeks by holding rallies in remote communities ahead of the 1999 national elections.
Buthelezi serves as home affairs minister in the government of national unity and has served as acting president of the country during the absence of both Mandela and Deputy President Thabo Mbeki.
However, he has been a thorn in Mandela's flesh since South Africa's transition to democracy in 1994.

The two leaders have traded harsh words over constant political fighting in KwaZulu-Natal, which has claimed over 14,000 lives since 1984, with Mandela accusing Buthelezi directly of being behind the conflict.
The Zulu chief is also at loggerheads with the ANC over his demand for greater autonomy for KwaZulu-Natal.
